items.title: [Bug]: skill-update backup handling can corrupt or silently lose skills (stale/orphaned .bak interactions)

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
### Bug Description

Follow-up to #34860, and distinct from #35131. That issue covered the backup cleanup failing silently. These are three remaining defects in how the bundled-update path in `tools/skills_sync.py` interacts with a `.bak` directory that already exists, which is exactly the artifact #34860 showed can be left behind. All three reproduce on current `main` (`9c50521`).

**A. A stale `.bak` poisons the next update's move and restore.**
`shutil.move(str(dest), str(backup))` is called without checking whether `backup` already exists. When it does (left over from any earlier failure), `shutil.move` moves the live skill *inside* the stale directory instead of replacing it. If the subsequent `copytree` fails, the restore path drags the stale junk back to `dest` with the user's real copy nested inside it, corrupting the skill. Its hash then no longer matches the manifest origin, so every later sync flags it "user-modified" and refuses to update it. The skill is permanently wedged.

**B. An orphaned `.bak` is misread as a user deletion (silent skill loss).**
If the process dies between `shutil.move(dest, backup)` and `shutil.copytree(...)` (crash, SIGKILL, power loss), the user's only copy of the skill sits in `dest.bak` and `dest` is gone. On the next sync the skill hits the branch that treats "in manifest but missing on disk" as a deliberate user deletion, so it's skipped forever. The skill silently disappears from discovery and is never restored or re-synced.

**C. A partially written `dest` blocks restore on failure.**
The restore guard is `if backup.exists() and not dest.exists()`. When `copytree` fails *after* creating `dest` (disk full, permission error mid-copy), `dest.exists()` is true, so the restore is skipped. The user keeps a broken partial skill, the `.bak` lingers, and the partial hash wedges the skill as "user-modified" on every later sync.

### Steps to Reproduce

Deterministic, no special platform required. From a repo checkout:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=. python3 - <<'EOF'
import shutil, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from unittest.mock import patch
from tools.skills_sync import sync_skills, _write_manifest, _dir_hash

tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
bundled = tmp / "bundled"; (bundled / "old-skill").mkdir(parents=True)
(bundled / "old-skill" / "SKILL.md").write_text("# v2")
skills = tmp / "skills"; skills.mkdir()
manifest = skills / ".bundled_manifest"

# user copy in sync with manifest origin
dest = skills / "old-skill"; dest.mkdir()
(dest / "SKILL.md").write_text("# v1")
with patch("tools.skills_sync.MANIFEST_FILE", manifest):
    _write_manifest({"old-skill": _dir_hash(dest)})

# (B) simulate a crash between move and copytree
shutil.move(str(dest), str(skills / "old-skill.bak"))

with patch("tools.skills_sync._get_bundled_dir", return_value=bundled), \
     patch("tools.skills_sync._get_optional_dir", return_value=tmp / "opt"), \
     patch("tools.skills_sync.SKILLS_DIR", skills), \
     patch("tools.skills_sync.MANIFEST_FILE", manifest):
    r = sync_skills(quiet=True)

print("dest exists:", dest.exists())                  # False, skill lost
print(".bak remains:", (skills / "old-skill.bak").exists())  # True
print("updated:", r["updated"], "skipped:", r["skipped"])
EOF
```

What I observe on current main (`9c50521`): the skill is treated as user-deleted, never recovered, and the `.bak` persists. Scenarios A and C reproduce the same way, by pre-creating a stale `old-skill.bak` (A) or by making `copytree` fail after creating `dest` (C). Regression tests for all three are in the linked PR.

### Expected Behavior

- An orphaned backup (dest missing) is recovered before classification, so an interrupted update self-heals instead of reading as a user deletion.
- A stale backup (dest present) is cleared before the move, so `shutil.move` replaces rather than nests, and restore-on-failure restores the pristine copy.
- On copy failure, a partially written `dest` is removed so the backup can actually be restored. No `.bak` remains and the skill is not wedged as "user-modified".

### Actual Behavior

See A/B/C in the description. In all three cases the user ends up with a lost, corrupted, or permanently un-updatable skill plus a lingering `.bak` directory.

### Affected Component

Skills (skill loading, skill hub, skill guard)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

```shell
N/A. I found these by code inspection and reproduced them deterministically from a clean source checkout of current main (script above). This isn't tied to a running install, so there are no logs or config to share. Happy to run `hermes debug share` against an install if that's useful.
```

### Operating System

Ubuntu 22.04 (source checkout; the bug is platform independent ordering logic)

### Python Version

3.10.12 (my repro environment; the defect is pure shutil and pathlib ordering, present regardless of Python version)

### Hermes Version

source checkout of current main, 9c50521 (pyproject version 0.16.0)

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The update transaction in `sync_skills()` (move, then copytree, then cleanup or restore; `tools/skills_sync.py` around lines 565 to 595 on current main) assumes a clean slate: no pre-existing `backup`, and an all-or-nothing `copytree`. Neither assumption holds after exactly the kind of failure #34860 documented, and the branch that handles "in manifest but missing on disk" has no notion of an in-flight update to recover.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

Three small ordering changes inside `sync_skills()`. I have a PR ready and will submit it right after filing this issue: recover orphaned backups before classification, clear a stale backup (using the existing `_rmtree_writable`) before `shutil.move`, and clear a partial `dest` before restoring the backup on copy failure. No behavior change on the happy path. Covered by three regression tests that fail on current `main`.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

items.title: [Bug]: send_message cannot resolve Signal group targets — missing Signal group pattern in _parse_target_ref (sender already supports group: chat_ids)

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
### Bug Description
 
The `send_message` tool cannot send to a Signal **group** by its group ID. Attempting
`send_message(target="signal:group:<base64GroupId>", message="hello")` (or the bare base64 ID)
fails with `Could not resolve` — even though the Signal sender in the same file already supports
group delivery via a `group:`-prefixed chat_id, and signal-cli confirms the account is a member
of the group.
 
This appears to be the same structural gap previously fixed for Slack (#15927, fixed in PR #15947)
and reported for BlueBubbles (#23409): `_parse_target_ref()` has no explicit-ID branch for Signal
group IDs, so they fall through to channel-directory resolution, which fails for any group that is
intentionally not in `SIGNAL_GROUP_ALLOWED_USERS`.
 
Note this breaks a legitimate security pattern: a **send-only** group (agent posts notifications,
but the group is deliberately not allowlisted so its members cannot command the agent). The only
current workaround that makes the directory resolve the group is allowlisting it — which enables
inbound from all group members and defeats the purpose.


### Environment
 
- Hermes Agent: v0.16.0 (2026.6.5) · upstream a8f404b2
- Install: native host install (install.sh), gateway as user service
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64
- Signal: signal-cli 0.14.5, native daemon `--http` mode (JSON-RPC + SSE)
- Signal config: `SIGNAL_ALLOWED_USERS` set; `SIGNAL_GROUP_ALLOWED_USERS` intentionally unset

###  Related issues
 
- #15927 — Slack: same structural bug ("Could not resolve" for raw channel IDs)
- #15947 — merged fix for Slack (parser branch + directory ID matching)
- #23409 — BlueBubbles: same structural bug, still open

### Steps to Reproduce
 
1. Signal platform configured and working (DMs work both directions).
2. The bot account is a member of a group. Confirmed via signal-cli JSON-RPC:
```
   curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/rpc \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"listGroups","id":1}'
   # → returns the group with "isMember": true
```
 
3. The group is **not** in `SIGNAL_GROUP_ALLOWED_USERS` (intentionally — send-only use case).
4. Ask the agent to call:
```
   send_message(target="signal:group:<base64GroupId>", message="test")
```
 
5. Observe:
```
   Tool send_message returned error (0.00s): {"error": "Could not resolve
   'group:<base64GroupId>' on signal.
   Use send_message(action='list') to see available targets."}
```
 
   The same failure occurs with the bare base64 ID and with a `group.`-prefixed form.

### Expected Behavior
 
`send_message(target="signal:group:<base64GroupId>", message="...")` with an explicit, valid
group ID should be treated as an explicit target (no channel-directory lookup required) and
delivered to that group — mirroring how explicit raw IDs are handled for Telegram and, since
#15947, for Slack. The message should arrive in the group, and the tool should return
`{"success": true, "platform": "signal", "chat_id": "group:<id>"}`.
 
This should work regardless of whether the group is present in `SIGNAL_GROUP_ALLOWED_USERS`,
since that variable gates **inbound** group access; an explicit outbound target should not
depend on it. (This is what enables the send-only group pattern described above.)

### Actual Behavior
 
The send is never attempted. `_parse_target_ref()` returns `is_explicit=False` for any
group-shaped ref, the target falls through to `resolve_channel_name()`, the directory lookup
fails (the group is not allowlisted, and the directory does not match raw IDs), and the tool
returns:
 
```
{"error": "Could not resolve 'group:<base64GroupId>' on signal.
Use send_message(action='list') to see available targets."}
```
 
The same error is returned for the bare base64 ID and the `group.`-prefixed form. Nothing is
delivered, and no send request reaches signal-cli (confirmed: no corresponding RPC activity in
the signal-cli daemon log).

### Affected Component

Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

Signal

### Debug Report

```shell
  Report       https://paste.rs/vJ6yX
  agent.log    https://paste.rs/COzf3
  gateway.log  https://paste.rs/nm8dw
```

### Operating System

Ubuntu 24.04

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

0.16.0

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)
 
Two findings in `tools/send_message_tool.py`:
 
1. `_send_signal()` **already supports groups** — it routes based on the chat_id prefix:
```python
   if chat_id.startswith("group:"):
       params["groupId"] = chat_id[6:]
   else:
       params["recipient"] = [chat_id]
```
 
2. But `_parse_target_ref()` has no Signal branch that recognizes a group ID as an explicit
   target. Signal group IDs are base64 (e.g. 44 chars ending in `=`) and do not match the
   phone-number pattern, so `is_explicit=False` is returned and `_handle_send()` falls through
   to `resolve_channel_name()`. The channel directory only contains allowlisted/known channels,
   so resolution fails and the send is never attempted — even though the delivery path one
   function below would handle it.

### Proposed Fix (optional)
 
Add a Signal branch to `_parse_target_ref()` that recognizes group-shaped refs and passes them
through with the `group:` prefix `_send_signal()` expects. Phone numbers/UUIDs fall through to
the existing handling unchanged:
 
```python
    if platform_name == "signal":
        ref = target_ref.strip()
        # Accept "group.<id>" as an alias for "group:<id>"
        if ref.startswith("group."):
            ref = "group:" + ref[len("group."):]
        # Explicit group target: "group:<base64GroupId>" or a bare base64 group id
        if ref.startswith("group:"):
            return ref, None, True
        if re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9+/]{40,}={0,2}", ref):
            return "group:" + ref, None, True
```
 
With this patch applied locally, `send_message(target="signal:group:<id>", ...)` delivers to the
group successfully, DM sends are unaffected, and the non-allowlisted group correctly remains
inbound-blocked.
 
A directory-side complement (matching by raw ID in `resolve_channel_name`, as done for Slack in
#15947) would also help, but the parser branch alone is sufficient for explicit IDs.

## Summary

`scripts/whatsapp-bridge/` has one unfixed critical vulnerability in `@whiskeysockets/baileys` after the recent `npm audit fix` (PR #44980). Tracking it here so it doesn't get lost.

## CVE

**GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg** — *Baileys has message upsert / hist sync spoofing and app state corruption when using maliciously crafted protocolMessage payload.*

- **Severity:** critical
- **Status:** no upstream fix available
- **Advisory:** https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
- **Affected:** `@whiskeysockets/baileys` 7.0.0-rc.1 through 7.0.0-rc.11

## Current state

`scripts/whatsapp-bridge/package.json` pins Baileys to a specific commit:

```
"@whiskeysockets/baileys": "WhiskeySockets/Baileys#01047debd81beb20da7b7779b08edcb06aa03770"
```

The bridge imports from `@whiskeysockets/baileys` in `bridge.js` and uses it as the sole transport for WhatsApp Web protocol (QR auth, message send/receive, end-to-end encryption handshake).

## Practical impact

- A malicious contact (or anyone who knows the user's phone number) can send a crafted `protocolMessage` payload that causes Baileys to either (a) accept a fake message upsert that didn't originate from the claimed sender, or (b) corrupt the local app-state sync.
- For an agent bridge that acts on incoming message content, this is a **message-spoofing primitive** — an attacker can make the agent believe a contact said something they didn't.
- Existing mitigation: `scripts/whatsapp-bridge/allowlist.js` restricts which senders the bridge will process, which substantially narrows the attack surface but doesn't eliminate it (a spoofed message can still appear to come *from* an allowlisted sender).

## Resolution path

1. **Monitor upstream.** Watch `WhiskeySockets/Baileys` main branch for a fix commit. When one lands past `01047deb`, bump the pin in `package.json` to that commit and re-audit.
2. **Evaluate Baileys forks.** Community successors like `@realvare/based-baileys` are an option if upstream maintenance stalls, but they carry their own supply-chain risk.
3. **Long-term:** pin Baileys to a tagged release once the maintainers publish a stable version that includes the fix, rather than a moving git commit.

## Action items

- [ ] Subscribe this issue to be notified when the advisory is updated (watch GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg on GitHub)
- [ ] Periodically re-run `npm audit` in `scripts/whatsapp-bridge/` to detect a fix
- [ ] When upstream ships a fix: bump pin, re-install, re-audit, smoke-test the bridge (QR auth + send/receive), open a follow-up PR

items.title: fix(send_message): reuse gateway Telegram HTTP transport config in standalone sends
items.body:
## Summary

Standalone Telegram sends used by cron final delivery do not reuse the gateway adapter's hardened HTTP transport configuration.

The live gateway path in `gateway/platforms/telegram.py` builds `HTTPXRequest` instances with the current Hermes-specific network behavior:
- proxy resolution via `TELEGRAM_PROXY`
- fallback-IP transport when direct Telegram DNS/routing is unreliable
- the tuned pool/connect/read/write timeout settings from `HERMES_TELEGRAM_HTTP_*`

The standalone send path in `tools/send_message_tool.py` still constructs a separate `Bot(...)` path, so cron jobs can finish successfully and then fail only at the final Telegram delivery step with `Telegram send failed: Timed out`, even though interactive Telegram usage works.

## Why this is a separate issue

This is not the same root cause as closed issue #38780.

- #38780 was about cron standalone delivery lacking delivery-level timeout protection and blocking job finalization.
- This issue is about the standalone Telegram sender bypassing the gateway adapter's transport/proxy/fallback configuration, so it times out on networks where the gateway path succeeds.

## Reproduction shape

1. Configure Hermes so live Telegram usage works through proxy or fallback-IP handling.
2. Run a cron flow that delivers through the standalone send path at the end of the job.
3. Observe the job complete, then fail at final Telegram delivery with a timeout from the standalone sender.

## Expected behavior

Standalone Telegram sends should use the same transport construction as the gateway adapter so cron delivery and live Telegram behavior stay aligned.

## Proposed direction

Extract one shared Telegram `HTTPXRequest` builder and reuse it in both paths.

That extends the parity principle already being pursued in:
- #20924
- #21777

items.title: Desktop: "New Session" button / Ctrl+N creates the chat in the launch profile instead of the active profile (app-global remote mode)
items.body:
﻿## Summary

When the Desktop app is connected to a single remote backend serving multiple profiles (app-global remote mode), creating a new chat via the sidebar **"New Session" button** or the **Ctrl/Cmd+N shortcut** silently creates the session in the **launch profile** (the backend's `active_profile`, typically `default`) â€” even when the user has explicitly selected a different profile in the profile rail and the sidebar is showing that profile's sessions.

Because the model picker is independent of the profile, the new chat keeps the model the user was using in the other profile, so everything *looks* right â€” but the session binds to the wrong profile's `state.db`, HERMES_HOME, SOUL.md, memories, and skills. Any cron jobs the agent creates in that conversation are registered in the wrong profile too (and deliver to that profile's channels). This caused real damage on our side twice before we traced it: an overnight autonomous task intended for an isolated "lab" profile ran inside the main profile, used its skills, and delivered to its Telegram home channel.

## Environment

- Desktop: Windows 11 build from `apps/desktop` at main `484f484c2` (2026-06-11); bug confirmed still present on `origin/main` as of 2026-06-12
- Connection: `connection.json` `mode: "remote"`, single remote URL, `profiles: {}` (app-global remote mode)
- Backend: Hermes Agent v0.16 (all-in-one container), 2 profiles: `default` (launch/active) + one named profile

## Steps to reproduce

1. Connect the Desktop to a remote backend that has a named profile besides `default` (backend `active_profile` = `default`).
2. Click the named profile's square in the rail (sessions list switches to it â€” you are "in" that profile).
3. Click the sidebar **"New Session"** button (or press Ctrl/Cmd+N).
4. Send any message.

**Expected:** the new session is created in the selected (active gateway) profile and persists to its `state.db`.

**Actual:** the session is created in the launch profile (`default`) â€” it appears under `default` in the session list and persists to the root `state.db`.

## Root cause

Three pieces interact:

1. Both new-chat entry points reset the next-chat profile to `null`:
   - `apps/desktop/src/app/chat/sidebar/index.tsx` (~line 818): `if (isNewSession) { $newChatProfile.set(null) }`
   - `apps/desktop/src/app/hooks/use-keybinds.ts` (~line 131, `'session.new'` handler): `$newChatProfile.set(null)`
   The comments at both sites say a plain new chat should "land in whatever profile the live gateway is on" / "target the current live profile".

2. `apps/desktop/src/app/session/hooks/use-session-actions.ts` (`createBackendSessionForSend`, ~line 380) **omits** the `profile` param when `$newChatProfile` is `null`:
   ```ts
   ...(newChatProfile ? { profile: newChatProfile } : {})
   ```

3. The server (`tui_gateway/server.py`, `session.create` handler, ~line 3342) interprets a missing `profile` as the **launch profile**:
   > "Omitted/own profile â†’ the launch profile (unchanged for single-profile and per-profile-remote setups)."

So `null` does **not** mean "current live profile" as the client comments intend â€” in app-global remote mode it means "launch profile", which is `default` regardless of `$activeGatewayProfile`. The paths that *do* set `$newChatProfile` (profile rail click â†’ `selectProfile`, the per-profile "+" in the All-profiles view â†’ `newSessionInProfile`, and the `/profile <name>` slash command) work correctly, which makes the button/shortcut failure intermittent-looking and hard for users to diagnose.

## Suggested fix

In `createBackendSessionForSend`, fall back to the live gateway profile instead of omitting the param:

```ts
const newChatProfile = $newChatProfile.get() ?? normalizeProfileKey($activeGatewayProfile.get())
```

(Server-side `_profile_home` already returns `None` for the launch profile, so always passing the resolved profile is a no-op for single-profile users.) Alternatively, change the two `set(null)` call sites to `set($activeGatewayProfile.get())` â€” either way makes the behavior match the existing comments.

## Impact

Multi-profile users separate profiles precisely to isolate memory, skills, channels, and autonomous jobs. This bug silently routes work â€” including cron creation and channel delivery â€” across that isolation boundary, with no visual indication until the agent identifies itself.

items.body:
Hi Hermes team,

Telegram Bot API 10.1 introduced Rich Messages, including `sendRichMessage`, `InputRichMessage`, `RichBlockTable`, `RichBlockTableCell`, headings, lists, collapsible sections, formulas, inline media, and support for bot messages up to 32,768 characters.

Official references:
- Telegram announcement: https://telegram.org/blog/watch-apps-and-more
- Bot API changelog: https://core.telegram.org/bots/api-changelog

This could significantly improve Hermes' Telegram UX for AI-generated structured output, especially analytical reports. Today, Hermes' Telegram adapter still relies on MarkdownV2/text messages and the 4096-character chunking path. For reports with tables, this often produces hard-to-read monospaced tables, many continuation messages, and higher risk of Telegram flood control.

A good first MVP could be:

1. Add an optional config flag, disabled by default, for example:
   `telegram.rich_messages.enabled: false`

2. Add a raw Bot API helper for `sendRichMessage`, without blocking on full `python-telegram-bot` typed support.

3. Support a conservative subset first:
   - headings
   - paragraphs
   - simple tables via `RichBlockTable`
   - maybe dividers/details later

4. Keep a strict fallback:
   if rich message sending fails for any reason, use the existing MarkdownV2/text send path.

5. Add a small structured-output renderer contract, for example:
   `title + summary + columns + rows -> Telegram Rich Message`
   This would make it useful for analytics and BI-style agents without requiring arbitrary rich formatting from the LLM.

6. Add tests for:
   - rich payload building
   - fallback behavior
   - disabled-by-default behavior
   - large-table handling

`python-telegram-bot` support for Bot API 10.1 is currently still in progress:
- https://github.com/python-telegram-bot/python-telegram-bot/issues/5261
- https://github.com/python-telegram-bot/python-telegram-bot/pull/5263

Because of that, a raw Bot API path behind a feature flag might let Hermes support Rich Messages earlier, while still allowing a later migration to PTB's typed API once it is released.

Use cases:
- financial summaries
- operational dashboards
- comparison tables
- incident reports
- AI-generated reports with clear sections and tables

This would make Telegram output much more readable and reduce message chunking for long structured responses.

## Bug Description

Kimi Code Plan supports vision capabilities, but Hermes' auto-detection logic routes vision requests to the wrong endpoint format, causing 404 errors.

## Current Behavior

When using Kimi Code Plan (`kimi-coding` provider) for vision tasks, Hermes routes to `https://api.kimi.com/coding` (Anthropic Messages format), which does not support OpenAI-style `image_url` content blocks.

The user must manually configure:
```yaml
auxiliary:
  vision:
    provider: custom
    base_url: https://api.kimi.com/coding/v1  # OpenAI-compatible endpoint
    api_key: 'sk-kimi-...'
    model: kimi-for-coding
```

## Expected Behavior

When the main provider is `kimi-coding` and the user has configured a Kimi Code Plan API key, Hermes should **auto-detect** that vision tasks need the OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`/coding/v1`) instead of the Anthropic endpoint (`/coding`).

## Root Cause

In `agent/auxiliary_client.py`:

1. `_PROVIDERS_WITHOUT_VISION` excludes `kimi-coding` entirely (line 343-345)
2. `_endpoint_speaks_anthropic_messages()` detects `api.kimi.com/coding` as Anthropic format, but the OpenAI-compatible `/coding/v1` endpoint is also caught by this detection
3. The credential pool stores `base_url: https://api.kimi.com/coding` (Anthropic) for `kimi-coding` provider

## Proposed Solution

Implement **strategy pattern** for base_url resolution:

1. **For vision tasks**: Auto-switch to `https://api.kimi.com/coding/v1` (OpenAI format)
2. **For text/chat tasks**: Keep using `https://api.kimi.com/coding` (Anthropic format)
3. **Remove `kimi-coding` from `_PROVIDERS_WITHOUT_VISION`** (already done in recent commits)
4. **Update credential pool**: Store both endpoints or auto-derive the correct one based on task type

### Code Changes Needed

```python
# In _resolve_task_provider_model() or similar:
if provider == "kimi-coding" and task == "vision":
    # Override base_url to OpenAI-compatible endpoint
    base_url = "https://api.kimi.com/coding/v1"

```

Or more generally, add provider-specific task routing:

```python
_PROVIDER_TASK_BASE_URLS = {
    "kimi-coding": {
        "vision": "https://api.kimi.com/coding/v1",
        "default": "https://api.kimi.com/coding",

}
```

items.title: [Feature]: Cross-Session Context Continuity — Session Chain & Auto-Summarization
items.body:
## Problem or Use Case

I use Hermes for long, multi-session development work. Two recurring pain points:

1. **`/compress` information loss**: When the context window fills up, compression may silently discard critical information — specific pitfalls encountered, why certain decisions were made, edge cases discovered. These aren't always captured in the final response but are essential for continuity.

2. **`/new` total context wipe**: Starting a new session means starting from zero. There's no mechanism to carry forward a summary of what was accomplished, what failed, and what's in progress. Every fresh session requires re-explaining the situation.

3. **No session traceability**: After 5-10 sessions, I can't easily look back to see "what did we do in session X that caused bug Y?"

**Real scenario**: Yesterday I spent 3 sessions debugging a deployment issue. Each `/new` meant starting fresh. By session 3 I'd forgotten why I chose approach A over B in session 1, and had to re-discover the same pitfall.

## Proposed Solution

A native **session chain** mechanism that:

### 1. Auto-summarization on `/new` (or `/clear`)
When the user starts a new session, Hermes optionally summarizes the current session before discarding it. The summary focuses on:
- Key decisions and their rationale
- Pitfalls encountered  
- Unfinished work / blockers

### 2. Session chain file
A persistent chain file tracks session history:
```
~/.hermes/session-chain/
├── chain.yaml (or chain.md)
│   sessions:
│     - id: abc123
│       date: 2026-06-12T20:15
│       summary: "Debugged nginx config. Key finding: AppArmor on Ubuntu 24.04..."
│     - id: def456  
│       date: 2026-06-12T22:30
│       summary: "Fixed proxy issue. Learned that..."
│       parent: abc123  # links to previous session
└── abc123.md         # Full dialogue record (optional)
```

### 3. Context injection on new sessions
When starting a new session (after `/new` or on first message), optionally inject the chain summary as context:
```
[Session Chain]
Previous session (abc123): Debugged nginx config. Pitfall: AppArmor blocks /tmp writes on 24.04. Workaround: use ~/ instead.
Two sessions ago (xyz789): Set up v2rayA proxy for VM.
---
User's message: ...
```

### 4. Slash command: `/chain` or `/continue`
- `/chain` — view session chain history
- `/chain inject on|off` — toggle context injection
- `/chain summarize` — manually trigger summarization

### Configuration
```yaml
session_chain:
  enabled: true
  auto_summarize_on_new: true      # auto-summarize before /new
  inject_context_on_new: true       # inject chain into next session
  max_chain_entries: 20             # limit chain length
  full_dialogue_save: false         # also save full conversation
  summary_prompt: |                 # customizable
    Summarize this session focusing on:
    1. Pitfalls and problems encountered
    2. Key decisions and their rationale
    3. Unfinished work
```

## Alternatives Considered

### Current hack (proof of concept)
I've already implemented a rough version by modifying Hermes source directly:
- Modified `cli.py` (~70 lines) and `commands.py` (+2 lines)
- Added `/jixu` command that summarizes, saves to chain file, and auto-news
- Uses `_pending_jixu_note` to inject chain context into next session

This works but is fragile — it's hardcoded, bypasses session DB, and breaks on `hermes update`. Full details: [local implementation notes]

**Why native support is better**: Native integration with state.db, proper config isolation, survives updates, and the Hermes team knows better where context boundaries should live.

### Skill-based approach
Could this be a skill? Partially — a skill could handle summarization prompts. But session lifecycle hooks (`/new`, context injection) require CLI-level integration. The data persistence (chain file) could be skill-managed.

## Feature Type
- CLI improvement

## Scope
- Medium (few files, < 300 lines)

## Contribution
- [ ] I'd like to implement this myself and submit a PR

(I'd need guidance on the preferred architecture — session lifecycle hooks vs CLI handler approach)

---

**Note**: I feel strongly about this feature. Session continuity is the #1 friction point in my daily Hermes workflow. Happy to provide more details about my use case or help test any implementation.

items.title: web_search/web_extract silently routes to Parallel.ai without user opt-in
items.body:
Commit e0e257171 (PR #43798) changed the default behavior of `web_search` and `web_extract` when no backend is configured. Previously, the default backend selection fell through to `"firecrawl"` (which would fail later at call time if no API key was set). Now it silently routes all traffic to Parallel's hosted Search MCP endpoint at `search.parallel.ai/mcp`, even when the user has set no API key and configured no backend.

Two follow-up commits (93764b93, 0a5762c7) hardened this default further to prevent override.

**Technical concerns**

1. **No opt-in, no consent**: A user who installs with no web configuration now has `web_search` and `web_extract` traffic sent to a third-party service automatically. There is no user prompt, warning, or configuration step. The outbound HTTP traffic to `search.parallel.ai` happens silently.

2. **No local/offline fallback**: The old default (`firecrawl`) still required an API key, so functionally the result was the same, the tools didn't work without configuration. Now they route silently instead of failing honestly. Now there is no way to use these tools locally without either (a) accepting third-party routing to Parallel, or (b) explicitly configuring a different backend like searxng. The only other zero-setup option, `ddgs`, is search-only and cannot fulfill `web_extract`.

3. **No key required**: `PARALLEL_API_KEY` is not needed. The free MCP path activates on any install with no web config. This means accidental routing is the default.

4. **Requested resolution**:
   - Option A: Restore error-on-missing-config behavior. Require explicit user configuration before routing to any external web backend.
   - Option B: Add a local/built-in HTTP fetch fallback so users without API keys have a working offline option and are not silently vendor-routed.

**Disclosure context**

The PR was merged by maintainer teknium1, incorporating work from contributor NormallyGaussian. NormallyGaussian's GitHub profile identifies them as "Currently at @parallel-web" and their name as Matt H, with commit email `mharris@parallel.ai` (now recorded in `scripts/release.py:AUTHOR_MAP`). The PR description and commit message name Parallel as the destination but do not disclose the author's employment at Parallel.ai.

This is a minor disclosure omission and the change is technically transparent about what it does, but the combination of (a) default third-party routing, (b) no consent mechanism, and (c) an undisclosed relationship with the vendor means the community has not evaluated this change with full context.

## Bug Description

When context compression creates a child session (rotating `session_id`), the standing `/goal` is lost because `state_meta` key `goal:<old_session_id>` is never migrated to `goal:<new_session_id>`.

## Root Cause

1. Compression changes `session_entry.session_id` in-place at `gateway/run.py:8638-8643`
2. The post-turn goal hook (`_post_turn_goal_continuation`) reads the **new** session_id from `get_or_create_session(source)` at line 7569
3. `GoalManager(session_id=new_sid)` calls `load_goal()` which queries `state_meta` for `goal:<new_sid>` → returns `None`
4. `is_active()` returns `False` → Ralph loop silently stops

## Reproduction

1. Set a `/goal` in a gateway session
2. Have a long enough conversation to trigger context compression
3. After compression, the goal loop stops — `_post_turn_goal_continuation` returns early because `is_active()` is `False` for the new session_id
4. `state_meta` still has `goal:<old_session_id>` with status=active, but nothing reads it

## Key Code Path

```
_handle_message_with_agent()
  └─ agent runs, triggers compression
  └─ line 8638: session_entry.session_id = new_sid  # in-place mutation
  
_post_turn_goal_continuation()  
  └─ line 7569: session_entry = get_or_create_session(source)  # returns entry with new_sid
  └─ line 9512: GoalManager(session_id=new_sid)
  └─ load_goal("goal:<new_sid>") → None  # state_meta has goal:<old_sid> not new_sid
  └─ is_active() → False → return  # goal loop broken
```

## Suggested Fix

Two complementary fixes:

### 1. Migrate goal on compression (primary)

After line 8638-8643 in `gateway/run.py`, copy the active goal to the new session:

```python
if agent_result.get("session_id") and agent_result["session_id"] != session_entry.session_id:
    _old_sid_for_goal = session_entry.session_id
    session_entry.session_id = agent_result["session_id"]
    self.session_store._save()
    # ... existing topic binding sync ...
    
    # Migrate active goal to new session
    try:
        from hermes_cli.goals import load_goal, save_goal
        _old_goal = load_goal(_old_sid_for_goal)
        if _old_goal and _old_goal.status == "active":
            save_goal(session_entry.session_id, _old_goal)
    except Exception:
        pass
```

### 2. Parent chain fallback in `_goal_still_active_for_session`

Walk the `parent_session_id` chain as a safety net:

```python
def _goal_still_active_for_session(self, session_id: str) -> bool:
    if not session_id:
        return False
    try:
        from hermes_cli.goals import GoalManager
        if GoalManager(session_id=session_id).is_active():
            return True
        # Walk parent chain
        if self._session_db is not None:
            cur = session_id
            for _ in range(10):
                row = self._session_db._conn.execute(
                    "SELECT parent_session_id FROM sessions WHERE id = ?", (cur,)
                ).fetchone()
                parent = row[0] if row else None
                if not parent:
                    break
                if GoalManager(session_id=parent).is_active():
                    return True
                cur = parent
        return False
    except Exception:
        return False
```

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.16.0 (git install)
- Gateway mode (Feishu platform)
- `auxiliary.goal_judge` uses auto (main model)
- Context compression is frequent in long quantitative research sessions

items.body:
While debugging intermittent desktop boot failures ("Hermes couldn't start … Timed out connecting to Hermes backend after 60000ms") I found several places where the dashboard backend does heavy synchronous work directly on the asyncio event loop, making the whole server unresponsive (all HTTP plus the gateway WS ready frame) for tens of seconds:

- `GET /api/cron/jobs` (profile=all) calls `profiles.list_profiles()` inline — filesystem scans + per-profile YAML parsing on the loop (37s on my machine before #44930, still ~2-4s after).
- `GET /api/model/options` — ~9s on the loop.
- MCP server connection at startup blocks the gateway-ready frame: a slow `connect_timeout` on one MCP server delays every client's WS handshake by that amount (server-side signature: `ws accepted` followed by `ws ready frame send failed` in the gateway log).

Evidence: a 1s curl pulse against `/api/status` goes from ~0.4s responses to total silence for ~50s the moment the desktop renderer boots (it fires these endpoints in parallel), then recovers. `sample` of the backend process shows the event loop inside synchronous `read_text`/`readdir`/YAML work within coroutines.

Environment: macOS 15 (Darwin 24.6), Python 3.11.15, 11 profiles, Hermes v0.16.0.

Suggested direction: wrap these handlers' bodies in `asyncio.to_thread(...)` (the cron path already serializes via `_CRON_PROFILE_LOCK`, a threading lock), and/or move MCP connection out of the WS-accept critical path. Happy to contribute if maintainers agree on the approach.

Related PRs for the two worst concrete instances: #44930 (alias scan reading large binaries), #44931 (renderer-side initial-connect retry so cold-start stalls don't fail boot).

items.title: Prompt is lost entirely when a turn's first response never completes (stall or client disconnect)

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

Hermes appears to commit the user's prompt to `state.db` together with the
first completed model response — not on receipt. If that first response never
completes, **nothing from the turn is persisted**: not the prompt, not the
partial response. The turn vanishes as if it never happened.

## Environment

- hermes-agent v0.16.0 (rolling `main`), macOS 15 (Apple Silicon)
- Model: GPT-5.5 via `openai-codex` provider
- Reproduced on both CLI chat and the gateway's OpenAI-compatible
  `/v1/chat/completions` (streaming)

## Reproduction (gateway streaming variant)

1. POST a streaming request to the gateway `/v1/chat/completions` with a
   prompt that takes a while to answer.
2. Disconnect the client mid-generation (e.g. `curl -m 3 ...`, or a mobile
   browser tab being suspended — that's how we hit it in practice).
3. Inspect `state.db` for the session.

**Expected:** the user message is persisted on receipt; the aborted/partial
assistant response is either persisted partially or marked aborted.
**Actual:** no record of the user message or the response. The session's
message history skips the turn entirely.

The CLI variant is the same with a turn whose first model response stalls
indefinitely: the prompt is never stored.

## Impact

Two user-facing failure modes, both observed in real use:

1. **Silent data loss on mobile.** Ask a question, background the browser
   while the agent is thinking, return: no answer, and no record the question
   was ever asked.
2. **Confabulation in later turns.** Because the turn is missing from the
   session store, follow-up questions hit an agent with a hole in its own
   history. With `session_search` available, the model fills the gap by
   guessing from older sessions — in our case it confidently conflated two
   different hardware chipsets after losing its own (correct) prior answer.
   The data loss converts into wrong answers downstream.

## Suggested direction

Persist the user message at receipt (with the turn opened in a pending
state), and finalize/mark-aborted when the response settles. That keeps the
transcript truthful even when streams die — which on mobile clients is
routine, not exceptional.

`docker_extra_args` defined in `config.yaml` is silently ignored when running via the gateway (Telegram/Discord). The `_terminal_env_map` dict in `gateway/run.py` (line ~922) is missing the `docker_extra_args` → `TERMINAL_DOCKER_EXTRA_ARGS` mapping, so the value never reaches `_get_env_config()` in `terminal_tool.py`. Sandbox containers are created without the flags.

This is the same class of bug as #5722 and #20537 (`docker_env` and `docker_forward_env` missing from `env_mappings`).

**Environment**

- NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10 GPU)
- Hermes installed from source at `~/.hermes/hermes-agent`
- Running via: `python -m hermes_cli.main gateway run --replace`
- Terminal backend: `docker`

**Config**

```yaml
terminal:
  backend: docker
  docker_image: nikolaik/python-nodejs:python3.11-nodejs20
  docker_extra_args:
    - "--gpus=all"
  container_cpu: 1
  container_memory: 5120
  container_disk: 51200
  container_persistent: true
```

**### Expected**

Dynamically created sandbox containers should have:
```
HostConfig.DeviceRequests = [{"Count": -1, "Capabilities": [["gpu"]]}]
```

**### Actual**

Sandbox containers created by the gateway have:
```
HostConfig.DeviceRequests = null
```

The config is loaded (confirmed via `sed -n '/^terminal:/,/^web:/p' ~/.hermes/config.yaml`) but never propagated.

**### Root cause**

`gateway/run.py` line ~922, `_terminal_env_map` has entries for `docker_image`, `docker_volumes`, `docker_env`, `docker_mount_cwd_to_workspace`, etc. — but **not** `docker_extra_args`.

`terminal_tool.py` line 1128 correctly reads:
```python
"docker_extra_args": _parse_env_var("TERMINAL_DOCKER_EXTRA_ARGS", "[]", json.loads, "valid JSON"),
```

But `TERMINAL_DOCKER_EXTRA_ARGS` is never set because the gateway bridge is missing.

### Fix

One line added to `_terminal_env_map` in `gateway/run.py`:

```python
"docker_extra_args": "TERMINAL_DOCKER_EXTRA_ARGS",
```

After this change + gateway restart + sandbox recreation, `docker inspect` shows `DeviceRequests` populated correctly and GPU is accessible inside the sandbox.

items.title: [Bug]: UnicodeDecodeError in copilot_acp_client.py _stdout_reader on Windows

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
### Bug Description

On Windows, Hermes crashes when the copilot ACP subprocess emits **UTF-8** characters (e.g. emojis). The `_stdout_reader` thread in agent/copilot_acp_client.py errors with a UnicodeDecodeError because of how the subprocess pipes are opened and decoded. `Popen` is called with `text=True` but without encoding, so Python uses the system codepage `(cp1252)`, which cannot decode certain UTF-8 bytes.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. On Windows, run Hermes with the Copilot provider configured (default).
2. Trigger image analysis or any flow that prints _emoji_ or _non-Latin_ characters (Hermes prints `'👁️ analyzing ...'` during vision analysis).
3. Hermes crashes with `UnicodeDecodeError` in `copilot_acp_client.py _stdout_reader` when iterating over `proc.stdout`.

### Expected Behavior

The subprocess _stdout/stderr pipes_ should be read as **UTF-8** regardless of Windows locale. If the Copilot CLI uses **UTF-8** output, Hermes must use `encoding='utf-8'` when opening the pipes to avoid crashes. The `_stdout_reader` loop should gracefully handle invalid bytes if necessary (errors='replace' or similar).

### Actual Behavior

`UnicodeDecodeError` in `copilot_acp_client.py` at the `_stdout_reader` loop when iterating over `proc.stdout.` Example traceback: 
`UnicodeDecodeError: 'charmap' codec can't decode byte 0x8d in position 7040: character maps to <undefined>`

### Affected Component

CLI (interactive chat), Other

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

```shell
Report       https://paste.rs/6Do1r
agent.log    https://paste.rs/HAbf0
gateway.log  https://paste.rs/elTP6
desktop.log   https://paste.rs/TzuhE
```

### Operating System

Windows_NT x64 10.0.26200

### Python Version

3.14.3

### Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.16.0 (2026.6.5) · upstream d62979a6
Project: C:\\Users\\ar271\\AppData\\Local\\hermes\\hermes-agent
Python: 3.11.15
OpenAI SDK: 2.24.0

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell
I can provide additional logs if helpful; the debug report links above contain the full agent.log and gateway logs.
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The root cause is an encoding mismatch when spawning the Copilot ACP subprocess. In `agent/copilot_acp_client.py`, the subprocess is started with `text=True` but without an explicit `encoding` argument, so Python uses the platform default encoding (`CP1252` on many Windows systems). When the Copilot CLI emits **UTF-8** bytes (for example, emojis or other characters outside `CP1252`), the stdout reader attempts to decode those bytes with `CP1252` and raises `UnicodeDecodeError`.

Concretely, the problematic call is in `_run_prompt`, where the process is created like:

```python
proc = subprocess.Popen(..., text=True, ...)
```

The fix is to pass an explicit encoding (e.g. `encoding='utf-8'`) or to read the streams in binary and decode with an error-safe strategy (e.g. `errors='replace'`) so that non-decodable bytes do not crash the reader thread.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

Add `encoding='utf-8'` to the `subprocess.Popen` call in `_run_prompt` (`agent/copilot_acp_client.py` line ~440). Optionally set `errors='replace'` or decode manually to avoid crashes on invalid bytes. Workaround: set `PYTHONUTF8=1` in the environment.
